set.detail:
The murder of Pertinax on 28 March 193 and the Praetorians' sale of the throne to Didius Julianus provoked three provincial armies to proclaim their commanders: Septimius Severus on the Danube (9 April), Pescennius Niger in Syria, and, in effect, Clodius Albinus in Britain. Severus neutralised Albinus by making him Caesar and marched on Rome, which fell without a battle; Julianus was killed on 1 June and Severus replaced the Praetorian Guard with Danubian legionaries.

The war against Niger (193-194) was fought in the east. Niger held Byzantium and tried to take Perinthus; Severus' generals crossed to Asia, defeating Niger's commander Asellius Aemilianus at Cyzicus and Niger himself near Nicaea, then pursued him through the Cilician Gates. At Issus, near the site of Alexander's victory, Niger was decisively defeated in 194 and killed fleeing towards the Euphrates. Byzantium held out until late 195 or 196 and was razed. Severus punished the cities that had backed Niger, subordinating Antioch to Laodicea, and divided Syria into Coele Syria and Syria Phoenice, then campaigned in 195 against the Osroenians, Adiabenians and Arabs who had supported Niger.

In 195-196 Severus named his son Caracalla Caesar, effectively disinheriting Albinus, who proclaimed himself Augustus and crossed to Gaul with the British army. After skirmishes, including a victory for Severus at Tinurtium, the decisive battle was fought near Lugdunum on 19 February 197, one of the largest in Roman history. Albinus died, Lugdunum was sacked, and Severus executed 29 senators and many provincials, confiscating vast estates for the res privata.

The war established the Severan dynasty and confirmed that the frontier armies, especially the Danubian legions, made emperors. Its consequences included the doubling of the Guard from the legions, pay rises, new legions and the division of large provinces to prevent rebellion. Cassius Dio and Herodian are the main narrative sources.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1988)

set.detail:
Severus' eastern wars had two phases. In 195, after defeating Niger, he crossed the Euphrates to punish the client kingdoms and Arab peoples that had supported his rival or attacked Roman garrisons: Osroene, Adiabene and the Arabs of northern Mesopotamia. Based at Nisibis, his generals ravaged the area and Severus took the titles Arabicus and Adiabenicus, while refusing the title Parthicus to avoid provoking the Arsacids. Osroene lost much of its territory, and a Roman administration was established around Nisibis.

In 197, while Severus was fighting Albinus, the Parthian king Vologaeses V invaded Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis, defended by Julius Laetus. Severus returned east in the summer, relieved the city, built a fleet on the Euphrates and sailed down the river past Dura, taking Seleucia, Babylon and finally Ctesiphon in late 197 or January 198. Dio claims 100,000 captives. On 28 January 198 he took the title Parthicus Maximus, made Caracalla Augustus and Geta Caesar. Lacking supplies, the army withdrew up the Tigris. Severus twice attacked Hatra, the fortified Arab city in the desert, in 198 and 199, but the city's archers and machines firing bitumen (Dio's 'naphtha') repelled him, and in the second siege his European troops refused to renew an assault after he had halted it to save the temple treasures.

The war resulted in the creation of the province of Mesopotamia, with legions I and III Parthica at Singara and Rhesaina and an equestrian prefect at Nisibis, extending the frontier to the Khabur and Jebel Sinjar. Severus then toured Syria and Egypt (199-200). The Arch of Septimius Severus in the Roman Forum (203) commemorates the campaign in narrative panels. Dio judged the annexation a costly mistake; in the longer term the humiliation of the Arsacids contributed to the Sasanian revolution of 224 and the far more dangerous wars of the third century.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Edwell, Between Rome and Persia (2008)

set.detail:
In 207 the governor of Britain reported serious incursions by the Caledonii and Maeatae and asked for reinforcements or the emperor. Severus arrived in 208 with Julia Domna, Caracalla, Geta, the Praetorians and vexillations from other armies, making Eboracum the imperial seat. Herodian adds that he wanted to remove his sons from the luxuries of Rome and toughen them with war. A large logistics base was established: the fort at South Shields (Arbeia) was converted into a supply depot with granaries, Cramond on the Forth was reoccupied, and a new legionary base of 24 hectares was built at Carpow on the Tay.

In 209 Severus, carried in a litter because of gout, and Caracalla advanced into Caledonia, building roads and causeways through forests and marshes. The enemy avoided battle, used ambushes and decoys, and Dio's figure of 50,000 Roman dead from hardship and harassment is a gross exaggeration. A peace was imposed, with the cession of territory, and in 210 the emperors took the title Britannicus. When the Maeatae and Caledonii revolted again, Severus ordered a war of extermination, quoting Homer, and Caracalla led the 210 campaign because his father was ill. Coins proclaim VICTORIAE BRITTANNICAE, and the Hadrian's Wall system was extensively rebuilt in these years, so that later writers credited Severus with building the Wall.

Severus died at York on 4 February 211. Caracalla made peace with the Caledonians, abandoned the forts beyond the Antonine line and returned to Rome with Geta. Whether Severus meant to conquer the whole island or to impose a punitive settlement remains debated. The war was followed by the division of Britain into two provinces and by a century of relative peace on the northern frontier, which some historians attribute to treaties and subsidies imposed after the campaigns.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, The Roman Government of Britain (2005)
Hodgson, Hadrian's Wall: Archaeology and History (2017)

set.detail:
Caracalla, obsessed with Alexander, prepared a war against Parthia from 214, wintering at Nicomedia and Antioch and deposing the kings of Osroene and Armenia; the Armenians defeated the Roman force sent against them. Parthia was divided between Artabanus IV and his brother Vologaeses VI. According to Dio, Caracalla asked to marry Artabanus' daughter, and when refused, invaded; Herodian tells a more dramatic story in which Artabanus accepted and Caracalla massacred the Parthian nobles at the wedding feast. In 216 the Roman army crossed the Tigris into Media and Adiabene, ravaged the countryside and desecrated the royal tombs of Arbela, scattering the bones. Caracalla wintered at Edessa, planning a new campaign.

On 8 April 217 he was murdered near Carrhae on Macrinus' orders. Artabanus, gathering a large army with cataphracts and armoured camels, demanded the rebuilding of the cities destroyed, restitution and the evacuation of Mesopotamia. Macrinus met him at Nisibis in the summer of 217 in a three-day battle. Herodian and Dio describe the Roman lines withstanding the cavalry, with caltrops scattered to cripple the horses and camels, and enormous losses on both sides, until the plain was covered with bodies; the result was indecisive. Macrinus then bought peace in 218 for some 200 million sesterces in gifts, returning prisoners but keeping Mesopotamia, while presenting it in Rome as a victory.

The war was the last between Rome and the Arsacids. The losses and humiliation it inflicted on Artabanus, who still faced his brother and rebellious vassals, helped Ardashir of Persis overthrow him in 224. For Rome, the unpopular peace and Macrinus' attempt to cut army pay contributed to his fall in 218 to Elagabalus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Dignas and Winter, Rome and Persia in Late Antiquity (2007)

set.detail:
Ardashir I, having crushed the Arsacids, attacked Roman Mesopotamia in 230, besieging Nisibis and raiding towards Syria and Cappadocia. Severus Alexander tried diplomacy; Herodian says Ardashir replied by sending 400 tall Persian nobles in splendid dress to demand that the Romans abandon Syria and Asia Minor as former Persian lands, and Alexander had them arrested and settled as farmers in Phrygia. Alexander came east in 231 with the Praetorians and troops from the Danube, but had to deal with mutinies, including one in Egypt and another among Syrian troops.

In 232 he launched a three-pronged invasion. The northern army marched through Armenia into Media and devastated the land, but suffered heavily in the mountains during the retreat. The southern army, advancing along the Euphrates towards Characene, was surprised and destroyed by Ardashir's main force. Alexander himself, with the central army, did not advance as planned, by illness or caution, and withdrew to Antioch, while the remnants of the northern army suffered in the winter. Herodian's account blames the young emperor and his mother for the failure; Latin sources (Aurelius Victor, Festus, the Historia Augusta) speak of a great victory over Ardashir, and Alexander took the title Persicus Maximus and celebrated a triumph in Rome in 233.

The truth probably lies between: both sides suffered heavy losses, and Ardashir did not attack again until after 235, when he took Nisibis and Carrhae. The war showed that the Sasanians were a far more formidable enemy than the late Arsacids, capable of fielding large armies and resisting Roman offensives, and forced Rome to keep strong forces in the east even when the Rhine and Danube came under attack, as happened in 233-234 when Alamannic raids called Alexander west.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2014)

set.detail:
In 233-234 Germanic peoples broke through the frontier in Upper Germany and Raetia, burning forts and villas; coin hoards end in that period. Severus Alexander, returning from Persia, gathered a large army at Mogontiacum in 234, including eastern archers and Osrhoene and Armenian troops, and built a pontoon bridge over the Rhine, but preferred to negotiate and pay subsidies. His murder in March 235 brought Maximinus to power.

Maximinus led a large offensive across the Rhine in 235. Herodian describes the army devastating the land for some 300-400 Roman miles, burning villages and crops, and a battle in a marsh where Maximinus rode into the swamp in pursuit of the enemy, fighting until his horse sank to its belly; he sent paintings of the battle to the Senate to be displayed before the Curia. For centuries historians doubted that Roman armies operated deep in Germany at this period. In 2008, however, archaeologists discovered a battlefield at the Harzhorn near Kalefeld in Lower Saxony, some 200 km beyond the limes, with over 2,700 objects, including catapult bolts, arrowheads, hipposandals, a pickaxe (dolabra) stamped LEG IIII S A, for legio IIII Flavia Severiana Alexandriana, and coins down to Severus Alexander, revealing a Roman army fighting its way through a pass on its return south around 235-236.

Maximinus took the title Germanicus Maximus and in 236-237 moved to Sirmium to fight Dacians and Sarmatians across the Danube, earning the titles Dacicus Maximus and Sarmaticus Maximus. The expense of these wars, met by confiscations and pressure on cities, provoked the revolt of 238 that ended his reign. The Harzhorn finds have transformed scholarly views of Roman-German relations in the third century, showing large-scale Roman offensives continuing long after the Augustan era.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Berger et al., "Die römisch-germanische Auseinandersetzung am Harzhorn", Germania 88 (2010)
Pöppelmann et al. (eds), Roms vergessener Feldzug (2013)

set.detail:
The year 238 saw six emperors. Early in the year a tax revolt at Thysdrus in Africa proclaimed the aged proconsul Gordian I and his son Gordian II. The Senate recognised them, declared Maximinus a public enemy and appointed twenty consulars to defend Italy. Within about three weeks Capelianus, governor of Numidia, defeated and killed Gordian II at Carthage, and Gordian I hanged himself. The Senate, now committed, elected two of the twenty, the soldier Marcus Clodius Pupienus Maximus and the aristocrat Decimus Caelius Calvinus Balbinus, as joint Augusti; when the plebs rioted, demanding a Gordian, they made the thirteen-year-old grandson of Gordian I, Gordian III, Caesar. Fighting broke out in Rome between the people and the Praetorians, who were besieged in their camp, and part of the city burned.

Maximinus marched from Sirmium into Italy, finding Emona deserted, and besieged Aquileia, which the consulars Rutilius Pudens Crispinus and Tullius Menophilus defended stubbornly; Herodian says the women gave their hair for bowstrings. Pupienus gathered troops at Ravenna. Maximinus' army, short of supplies and fearing for families held hostage in Italy, mutinied, and soldiers of II Parthica killed Maximinus and his son. Pupienus entered Aquileia, then returned to Rome. The two senatorial emperors quarrelled, and after a reign of 99 days (Chronograph of 354) the Praetorians, resentful of the Senate's choice, seized them in the palace, dragged them through the streets and killed them, proclaiming Gordian III sole emperor.

The chronology is notoriously uncertain, with modern reconstructions ranging from January to August. The war revealed the Senate's capacity to act, but also the army's determination to choose emperors. It also left Africa without its legion, III Augusta being disbanded, and gave the Goths and Carpi the opportunity to sack Histria.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Peachin, "Once More AD 238", Athenaeum 67 (1989)
Drinkwater, in CAH XII2 (2005)

set.detail:
In the late 230s the Sasanians took advantage of the Roman civil wars to seize Nisibis and Carrhae (c. 235-238) and, in 240-241, Hatra, the Arab city that had resisted Trajan, Severus and Ardashir and had become a Roman ally with a Roman garrison. Shapur I, crowned co-ruler around 240, threatened Syria. In Rome, Gordian III and his prefect Timesitheus prepared a great expedition. In 242 Gordian opened the doors of the temple of Janus, a rare ceremony, and led the army east through the Balkans, fighting Goths, Sarmatians and Alans en route.

In 243 the Romans recovered Carrhae and Nisibis and defeated Shapur at Rhesaina, a victory Gordian reported to the Senate. Timesitheus died of illness soon afterwards and was replaced by Philip. The army pressed on down the Euphrates towards Ctesiphon, but early in 244 it met Shapur at Misiche, near Fallujah. Shapur's inscription claims a great victory in which Gordian was killed and the Roman army destroyed, after which the Romans made Philip emperor. Roman sources speak only of Gordian's death, attributing it to Philip's intrigues, and record the cenotaph raised at Zaitha.

Philip made peace quickly, paying 500,000 denarii according to the Persian inscription and apparently abandoning Roman support for Armenia, though he kept Mesopotamia. Coins proclaim PAX FUNDATA CUM PERSIS. Shapur commemorated the war in his reliefs at Bishapur and Naqsh-e Rostam, showing Philip kneeling and Gordian's corpse. The Greek, Middle Persian and Parthian versions of the ŠKZ inscription and Roman literary sources give irreconcilable accounts, a classic problem of third-century historiography. The peace lasted until about 252, when Shapur accused Rome of interfering in Armenia and resumed war.

scholarship: Kettenhofen, Die römisch-persischen Kriege des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1982)
Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)

set.detail:
After Philip stopped paying subsidies and the Danube army was weakened by revolts and the proclamation of Decius in 249, a large coalition led by the Gothic king Cniva, including Carpi and others, crossed the Danube in 250. One group besieged Novae and was repulsed by Trebonianus Gallus, governor of Moesia; another, under Cniva, moved to Nicopolis ad Istrum, where Decius defeated it. Cniva crossed the Haemus mountains and surprised Decius' army at Beroe (Augusta Traiana), routing it. The Goths then besieged Philippopolis, the capital of Thrace, whose governor Titus Julius Priscus proclaimed himself emperor, perhaps with Gothic support; the city fell and was sacked, with many killed and nobles taken prisoner.

In the spring of 251, as the Goths withdrew north with booty and captives, Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus tried to intercept them. In June 251 at Abritus in Moesia Inferior the Goths, using a marsh as a trap, defeated the Romans; both emperors were killed and Decius' body was never found. Trebonianus Gallus, proclaimed by the army, allowed the Goths to return home with their spoils and prisoners and promised annual payments, a treaty that Roman writers considered shameful. Plague broke out at the same time.

The war opened two decades of Gothic invasions by land and sea, culminating in the great raids of 267-270. Jordanes, drawing on Dexippus, and Zosimus are the main sources, along with fragments of Dexippus' Scythica, recently supplemented by the Vienna palimpsest that describes fighting around Philippopolis and Thermopylae. Archaeology shows destruction layers and coin hoards across Moesia and Thrace. Decius' death, the first of a Roman emperor fighting a foreign enemy, was seen by Christians as punishment for his persecution.

scholarship: Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

set.detail:
Shapur I's second and third campaigns against Rome were the most destructive in the history of the eastern frontier. In 252, after accusing Rome of wronging Armenia, Shapur invaded and, according to his inscription, destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 at Barbalissos on the Euphrates, then devastated Syria, Cilicia and Cappadocia, capturing 37 cities including Antioch, probably in 253, where the renegade Mariades helped him. Huge numbers of captives were deported to Persia. Uranius Antoninus, a priest of Emesa, repelled the Persians from his city and struck his own coins. Shapur withdrew with his booty.

Valerian came east in 254 or 256 and restored Antioch, but the Persians took Dura-Europos around 256, besieging it with mines and ramps, and raided again. In 259-260 Shapur besieged Edessa and Carrhae. Valerian, with an army weakened by plague, advanced to relieve them and was captured, either in battle or during negotiations, with his praetorian prefect, senators and soldiers. Persian columns then invaded Cilicia, Cappadocia and Lycaonia, taking Tarsus, Caesarea and other cities, until Valerian's officer Ballista surprised them near Pompeiopolis and Corycus and Odaenathus harried their retreat across the Euphrates.

After 260 the defence of the east fell to Odaenathus of Palmyra, who, after destroying the usurper Quietus in 261, attacked Persia in 262 and again around 266, recovering Mesopotamia and reaching Ctesiphon. The war cost Rome an emperor, its largest eastern city and tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians; it led to the Palmyrene ascendancy and the division of the empire. For Persia, the deportees brought Roman techniques and Christianity, shaping the development of cities such as Gundeshapur and Bishapur and the Christian church of the Sasanian empire.

scholarship: Kettenhofen, Die römisch-persischen Kriege des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1982)
Potter, Prophecy and History in the Crisis of the Roman Empire (1990)

set.detail:
After the Gothic war of 249-251, Gothic and related peoples (Boranoi, Heruli, Carpi, Urugundi) launched repeated invasions by land and by sea. In 253 Aemilianus, governor of Moesia, defeated a Gothic band and was proclaimed emperor. Around 254 Goths besieged Thessalonica, provoking the refortification of the Isthmus and Athens. Seaborne raids began when peoples north of the Black Sea forced or persuaded the Bosporan Kingdom to provide ships: around 255-256 the Boranoi attacked Pityus, repulsed by its commander Successianus, and then sacked Trapezus with its large garrison; in 257 Goths sailed along the western Black Sea coast and crossed into Bithynia, sacking Chalcedon, Nicomedia, Nicaea, Cius, Apamea and Prusa. Gregory Thaumaturgus' Canonical Letter discusses Christians in Pontus who collaborated with the raiders.

In 262 Goths burned the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. The greatest invasion came in 267-268, when Heruli and Goths with a reported 500 ships entered the Aegean, sacking Cyzicus, the islands, Corinth, Argos, Sparta and Athens, where Dexippus led a resistance; Gallienus defeated them on the Nestus in 268. In 268-269 an even larger land and sea invasion besieged Thessalonica and Cassandreia; Claudius II crushed it near Naissus, earning the title Gothicus, and plague and famine destroyed the survivors, while a fleet raided Crete, Rhodes and Cyprus. In 270 Goths attacked Anchialus and Nicopolis.

In 271 Aurelian crossed the Danube and defeated the Goths, killing their leader Cannabaudes with 5,000 men, and then withdrew from Dacia, shortening the frontier. The Gothic threat subsided for half a century, and many Goths were settled in the empire or enrolled in the army. The invasions transformed the Balkans and Greece, shrinking cities behind new walls and destroying monuments, and mark the emergence of the Goths as a major power north of the Danube. Zosimus, Dexippus (including the newly found Vienna fragments), Jordanes, Syncellus and Zonaras are the main sources.

scholarship: Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Mitthof et al. (eds), Die neuen Dexipp-Fragmente (2020)

set.detail:
In the late 250s, while Gallienus fought on the Danube and Valerian in the east, Germanic peoples from the upper Rhine and Danube, later known collectively as Alamanni, together with the Juthungi (named by Dexippus as a separate people), broke through the Upper German-Raetian limes, which was abandoned around 260. Around 259-260 a large force invaded Italy, reaching as far as Rome, where the Senate armed the populace. Gallienus defeated them near Milan. An altar found in Augsburg in 1992 records that on 24-25 April 260 the governor of Raetia, Simplicinius Genialis, defeated 'barbarians of the Semnones or Juthungi' returning from Italy with thousands of Italian captives, whom he freed. The inscription is dated by the consuls of Postumus, showing that Raetia had joined the Gallic Empire.

In 268 Claudius II defeated the Alamanni at Lake Benacus (Garda). In 270-271 the Juthungi invaded Italy again. After an initial defeat near the Danube and failed negotiations described by Dexippus, Aurelian was defeated in an ambush near Placentia; panic spread in Rome, where riots and conspiracies broke out. Aurelian then defeated the invaders at Fanum Fortunae on the Metaurus and near Ticinum, destroying them. The Aurelian Walls of Rome, begun in 271, were the lasting response.

These invasions ended the Roman presence in the Agri Decumates, between the upper Rhine and Danube, which were occupied by Alamannic groups; the new frontier ran along the Rhine, Lake Constance, the Iller and the Danube, later fortified by Diocletian and Valentinian (the Danube-Iller-Rhine limes). Italy itself, untouched by invasion for centuries, became vulnerable, prompting the walling of its cities. John Drinkwater's study stresses that the Alamanni were a loose collection of groups, and that Roman sources often exaggerated their unity and threat.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)
Bakker, "Raetien unter Postumus", Germania 71 (1993)

set.detail:
The Gallic Empire began in 260 when the Rhine army proclaimed Postumus, who killed Gallienus' son Saloninus at Cologne. Its rulers controlled Gaul, the Germanies, Britain, Spain and briefly Raetia. Gallienus, occupied elsewhere, attempted only one serious campaign, around 265, when he and his general Aureolus defeated Postumus but failed to take the city where he took refuge, Gallienus being wounded by an arrow. In 268 Aureolus, commanding Gallienus' cavalry at Milan, rebelled, perhaps initially in Postumus' name, but Postumus did not intervene, and Aureolus was killed after Gallienus' murder.

The Gallic Empire weakened after 269. Postumus was killed by his troops after suppressing the usurper Laelianus at Mogontiacum; his successor Marius reigned briefly, then Victorinus, a former praetorian prefect. Spain and Gallia Narbonensis returned to Claudius II, whose general Julius Placidianus occupied the Rhône valley, and in 269-270 the city of Augustodunum (Autun), which had declared for Claudius, was besieged by Victorinus for seven months and sacked, a disaster recalled in a panegyric of 298 for the city's restoration. Victorinus was murdered in 271 by an officer whose wife he had seduced; his mother Victoria secured the succession for Tetricus, governor of Aquitania, who later appointed his son Tetricus II Caesar. A usurper named Domitianus also rose and fell around 271.

After reconquering the east, Aurelian invaded Gaul in 274 and defeated Tetricus at Châlons. Tetricus, who according to the Latin tradition had betrayed his army, was spared, paraded in Aurelian's triumph and given an administrative post in Italy. The end of the Gallic Empire reunited the west, but Germanic raids devastated Gaul in 275-276. John Drinkwater's study established that the Gallic emperors were Roman rulers responding to local needs, not separatists.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)

set.detail:
After Odaenathus' murder in 267-268, his widow Zenobia, ruling for their son Vaballathus, expanded Palmyrene control. In 270, after Claudius II's death, the general Zabdas conquered Egypt, killing the prefect Tenagino Probus, and Palmyrene forces occupied Arabia and much of Asia Minor as far as Ancyra. At first coins presented Vaballathus as king and Roman official under Aurelian, but in 272 he took the title Augustus.

Aurelian marched east in 272 through Asia Minor, recovering Ancyra and taking Tyana, which he spared, according to the Historia Augusta, after seeing a vision of Apollonius of Tyana, the city's famous sage. Near Antioch, at Immae, Zabdas' heavy cavalry were lured into pursuing Aurelian's light cavalry until exhausted and then destroyed; Zabdas withdrew to Emesa, using a lookalike of Aurelian to pretend Aurelian had been captured, to escape Antioch. Aurelian defeated the Palmyrenes again near Emesa, where his heavy infantry, including Palestinian club-men, broke the Palmyrene cavalry. He then besieged Palmyra; Zenobia fled for Persia but was captured at the Euphrates, and the city surrendered. Egypt was recovered by Aurelian's general, the future emperor Probus according to some sources. After a trial at Emesa, Longinus was executed.

In 273 Palmyra revolted again, killing the Roman garrison and proclaiming Septimius Antiochus; at the same time unrest broke out in Alexandria, where a certain Firmus is said to have led a revolt. Aurelian returned, sacked Palmyra and suppressed the Egyptian rising, destroying the Bruchion quarter of Alexandria. Palmyra never regained its commercial importance, though Diocletian later built a legionary camp there. The war reunited the eastern provinces with the empire and is narrated in detail by Zosimus and the less reliable Historia Augusta.

scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

set.detail:
Mausaeus Carausius, a Menapian from the Rhine delta of humble birth and a skilled sailor, was appointed by Maximian to command a fleet at Gesoriacum to clear the Channel of Frankish and Saxon pirates. Accused of letting the raiders plunder before intercepting them and keeping the booty, he was condemned to death and in 286 or 287 proclaimed himself emperor, controlling Britain and part of northern Gaul with its fleet and a legion. In 289 Maximian's attempt to invade Britain with a newly built fleet failed, perhaps because of storms, and Carausius styled himself colleague of the two Augusti, issuing coins with the legend 'Carausius and his brothers'. His coinage, of good silver, was full of Virgilian allusions, including RSR and INPCDA, abbreviations of lines from the Eclogues.

In 293 Constantius, newly made Caesar, besieged Gesoriacum, blocking its harbour with a mole, and took it, then cleared the Rhine delta of Carausius' Frankish allies. Shortly afterwards Carausius was murdered by his finance minister (rationalis) Allectus, who reigned for three years. In 296 Constantius invaded Britain with two fleets. One, under the praetorian prefect Asclepiodotus, landed under cover of fog, possibly near Southampton, burned its ships and defeated and killed Allectus somewhere inland. Constantius, delayed by weather, reached London in time to save the city from looting by Allectus' Frankish mercenaries. The gold medallion of Arras shows Constantius welcomed at the gates of London as 'restorer of the eternal light'.

The revolt highlighted the importance of naval power in the North Sea. The forts of the 'Saxon Shore', such as Portchester and Richborough, were built or improved around this time, perhaps partly by Carausius. Britain was divided into four provinces after the reconquest.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Casey, Carausius and Allectus: The British Usurpers (1994)
Williams, Carausius (2004)

set.detail:
In 293 Narseh, a son of Shapur I, overthrew the young Bahram III and became King of Kings; his inscription at Paikuli records his rise. Around 296 he invaded Armenia, expelling Tiridates III, Rome's ally, and then Roman Mesopotamia and Syria. Diocletian, in Egypt suppressing the revolt of Domitius Domitianus, sent Galerius against him. In 296 or 297 Galerius, with a small army, was defeated between Callinicum and Carrhae. The Latin sources tell that Diocletian then humiliated him by making him march a mile in front of his carriage in his purple robe.

In 298 Galerius returned with a new army of veterans and recruits from Illyricum and Moesia and attacked through Armenia, where the terrain and population favoured him. After personally reconnoitring the enemy camp, he surprised Narseh's army and routed it; Narseh fled wounded, and his wives, sisters, children, nobles and treasury were captured. Galerius then advanced into Media and Adiabene and possibly took Ctesiphon, while Diocletian secured Mesopotamia. Narseh sent his envoy Apharban to beg for the return of his family, comparing Rome and Persia to the two eyes of the world.

The Peace of Nisibis (299) gave Rome five regions east of the Tigris, recognition of its control over Armenia and Iberia, and Nisibis as the single trading post. It was the most favourable treaty Rome ever obtained from Persia and kept the eastern frontier quiet for almost forty years. Galerius' victory was celebrated on his arch at Thessalonica. Diocletian built new fortifications along the frontier, including the Strata Diocletiana. The main sources are Eutropius, Festus, Aurelius Victor, Lactantius, Petrus Patricius and Zonaras, along with the Arch of Galerius and Narseh's Paikuli inscription.

scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
Humbach and Skjaervø, The Sassanian Inscription of Paikuli (1978-83)

set.detail:
The Tetrarchic succession of 305, which excluded the sons of Maximian and Constantius, collapsed within eighteen months. In July 306 the army at York proclaimed Constantine; Galerius recognised him as Caesar. In October 306 the Praetorians and people of Rome proclaimed Maxentius, and his father Maximian returned to power. In early 307 Severus, now Augustus of the west, invaded Italy, but his troops deserted to Maximian, and he surrendered at Ravenna and was later forced to commit suicide. Maximian secured Constantine's support by marrying his daughter Fausta to him and granting him the title Augustus. In summer 307 Galerius invaded Italy but, unable to besiege Rome, withdrew.

In April 308 Maximian tried to depose Maxentius and fled to Constantine. At the conference of Carnuntum (November 308) Diocletian, briefly out of retirement, Galerius and Maximian agreed that Licinius would be Augustus of the west, Constantine and Maximinus Daia Caesars, and Maximian would retire again. The arrangement failed: Maximinus and Constantine took the title Augustus, Africa revolted against Maxentius under Domitius Alexander (308-310), and in 310 Maximian rebelled against Constantine at Arles and died at Massilia. Galerius died in 311 after issuing his edict of toleration, and Licinius and Maximinus divided his territories.

In 312 Constantine invaded Italy, defeating Maxentius' forces at Turin, Brescia and Verona and finally at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October, where Maxentius drowned. In 313 Licinius, now allied with Constantine, defeated Maximinus at Tzirallum (Campus Ergenus) near Adrianople on 30 April; Maximinus fled to Tarsus and died there. The wars left Constantine master of the west and Licinius of the east, and destroyed the Tetrarchic system. Lactantius' De Mortibus Persecutorum, Eusebius, the Origo and Zosimus are the main sources.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

set.detail:
The alliance between Constantine and Licinius sealed at Milan in 313 broke down within a few years. The first war, dated by most scholars to 316 (some argue 314), began when Constantine proposed that his brother-in-law Bassianus be made Caesar over Italy; Bassianus was implicated in a plot with Licinius' agent Senecio and executed. Constantine invaded Licinius' territory and won a hard-fought battle at Cibalae in Pannonia on 8 October 316. Licinius retreated to Thrace, proclaimed his general Valens co-emperor, and fought a second, indecisive battle at the Campus Ardiensis (Mardia) in Thrace. In the peace concluded at Serdica on 1 March 317, Licinius ceded all his European provinces except Thrace, Valens was executed, and three Caesars were proclaimed: Constantine's sons Crispus and Constantine II and Licinius' infant son Licinius II.

Relations remained tense. Licinius increasingly restricted Christians in his territories, and Constantine's pursuit of Sarmatians in 322 and Goths in 323 into Licinius' Thrace provided a pretext. In 324 Constantine invaded with an army and a fleet built at Thessalonica. On 3 July 324 he defeated Licinius at Adrianople; Crispus destroyed Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont, forcing Licinius to abandon Byzantium, which was besieged. Licinius crossed to Asia and named Martinianus co-emperor, but on 18 September Constantine crushed him at Chrysopolis. Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia and was executed in 325.

The wars made Constantine sole emperor, enabling him to found Constantinople, call the Council of Nicaea and apply his Christian policies across the empire. Christian writers, especially Eusebius, presented the conflict as a holy war against a persecutor, with the labarum leading Constantine's army. Modern historians emphasise the dynastic and political motives. The dating of the first war and the sequence of events in 316-317 rest on the Origo Constantini and fragmentary sources.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Bleckmann, "Constantine, Rome, and the Christians", in Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006)

set.detail:
In the later years of his reign Constantine reasserted Roman power north of the Danube. In 328 he built a stone bridge across the river between Oescus and Sucidava, some 2.4 km long, and established bridgeheads and forts on the north bank, such as Daphne. When the Tervingian Goths attacked the Sarmatians, Rome's clients in the Banat, Constantine sent his son Constantine II against them. On 20 April 332 the Romans won a great victory; the Origo says that nearly 100,000 Goths died of hunger and cold. A treaty followed by which the Goths, under their leader Ariaric, gave hostages, including his son, and supplied troops to the Roman army in return for subsidies and trading rights. Eusebius and Julian later describe Constantine boasting of having recovered Dacia, and coins proclaim GOTHIA and VICTORIA GOTHICA.

In 334 the Sarmatians' former slaves, the Limigantes, rose against their masters, the Argaragantes, and drove them out. Constantine admitted some 300,000 Sarmatian refugees of all ages and sexes, according to the Origo and Eusebius, and settled them in Thrace, Scythia, Macedonia and Italy, a mass resettlement that foreshadowed later admissions of barbarian peoples. Constantine took the titles Gothicus and Sarmaticus Maximus.

The treaty of 332 brought a generation of peace with the Tervingi, who remained Roman allies until their support for Procopius in 365. It also opened the way for Christian missions: Ulfilas, of Cappadocian descent, was consecrated bishop of the Goths in 341. Peter Heather sees the 332 treaty as a model of Roman client management; others debate whether the Goths were made foederati in a formal sense. Constantine's interest in the Danube region also underlay his plans for the Persian war that were interrupted by his death.

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)

set.detail:
Shapur II, who rejected the peace of 299, prepared war in the 330s; Constantine was planning a counter-offensive when he died in 337. Constantius II, ruling the east, defended the Mesopotamian frontier for over twenty years. Shapur besieged Nisibis in 338 for 63 days (in Christian tradition saved by the prayers of Bishop Jacob), again in 346, and in 350 for some four months, damming the river Mygdonius to flood the plain and batter the walls; each siege failed, as celebrated in Ephrem's Carmina Nisibena. Festus says that Constantius fought nine major battles against the Persians. The most famous was the night battle near Singara (344 or 348), in which the Romans stormed the Persian camp after defeating Shapur's army in the field, but, disordered by plundering, were counter-attacked at night and lost heavily; Shapur's son was captured and killed.

In the 350s Shapur was occupied with nomads on his eastern frontier, and Constantius with the civil war against Magnentius. In 358 Shapur, now allied with the Chionites, demanded the return of Mesopotamia and Armenia, claiming in a letter all lands up to the Strymon. In 359 he invaded with the guidance of the Roman defector Antoninus and took Amida after a siege of 73 days, described by Ammianus. In 360 he took Singara and Bezabde, deporting their garrisons; Constantius failed to retake Bezabde. As Constantius prepared to march against Julian, who had been proclaimed Augustus in Gaul, he died in 361.

The war was largely a war of sieges, in which Persian siege technology, elephants and cataphracts met Roman fortifications and field armies. It ended inconclusively, but the loss of Amida, Singara and Bezabde left the frontier weakened before Julian's invasion of 363. Ammianus, Julian's panegyrics of Constantius, Festus and Libanius' Oration 59 are the main sources.

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)
Dignas and Winter, Rome and Persia in Late Antiquity (2007)

set.detail:
On 18 January 350 Flavius Magnentius was proclaimed emperor at Augustodunum, and Constans was killed fleeing to Spain. Magnentius secured Gaul, Britain, Spain, Africa and Italy. In Rome Constantine's nephew Nepotianus proclaimed himself on 3 June 350 but was killed after 28 days by Magnentius' troops, who massacred his supporters. In Illyricum the general Vetranio was proclaimed on 1 March, perhaps on the initiative of Constantina to prevent the Danube army from joining Magnentius; at Naissus on 25 December 350 Constantius addressed the two armies and Vetranio laid down his purple, retiring to Prusa with a pension.

Constantius, who had left the Persian front, refused Magnentius' offers of an alliance. In 351 Magnentius invaded Pannonia, took Siscia and threatened Sirmium. On 28 September 351 Constantius defeated him at Mursa, after Silvanus had deserted to him, in a battle that cost, according to Zonaras, 54,000 lives. Magnentius retreated to Aquileia and the Julian Alps. In 352 Constantius recovered Italy, and Magnentius withdrew to Gaul, where Constantius stirred up the Alamanni against him. In 353 Constantius forced the passes of the Cottian Alps and defeated Magnentius at Mons Seleucus near Gap; Magnentius killed himself at Lugdunum on 10 August 353, and his brother and Caesar Decentius hanged himself at Senones on 18 August.

A harsh purge followed, led by the notary Paul, nicknamed 'the Chain', who hunted Magnentius' supporters in Britain, and by the prefects, which Ammianus describes in his first surviving book. The war reunited the empire under Constantius but devastated the western field army, opening the Rhine to Frankish and Alamannic invasions, and led to the appointment of Gallus and then Julian as Caesars.

scholarship: Drinkwater, "The Revolt and Ethnic Origin of the Usurper Magnentius", Chiron 30 (2000)
Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)

set.detail:
After the civil war against Magnentius, during which Constantius encouraged the Alamanni to attack the usurper, the Rhine frontier collapsed. Franks and Alamanni overran the Rhineland, and in 355 the Franks took Cologne; the murder of the general Silvanus left Gaul without a commander. Constantius appointed his cousin Julian Caesar on 6 November 355 and sent him to Gaul with a small force. In 356 Julian marched from Vienne to Autun, Auxerre, Troyes and Reims, defeated the Alamanni at Brocomagus, recovered Cologne and made peace with the Franks, but was besieged at Sens during the winter.

In 357 a planned pincer movement failed when Barbatio, coming from Italy, was defeated near Augst, but in August Julian defeated a coalition of seven Alamannic kings under Chnodomarius at Argentoratum (Strasbourg), the greatest Roman victory over Germans in the fourth century. That winter he besieged 600 Franks in two forts on the Meuse. In 358 he accepted the submission of the Salian Franks in Toxandria, drove off the Chamavi, restored the Rhine route for grain from Britain, crossed the river and forced the kings Suomarius and Hortarius to return captives and supply materials. In 359 he crossed near Mogontiacum and compelled further kings, including Macrianus, Hariobaudes and Vadomarius, to make peace and release 20,000 prisoners. In 360 he attacked the Frankish Attuarii across the lower Rhine, and in 361 he arrested Vadomarius for raiding Raetia.

Julian's victories restored Roman control of the Rhine and made him a popular commander; his own account in the Letter to the Athenians and Ammianus' detailed narrative (books 15-21) present him as a model general, while Libanius' funeral oration praises him extravagantly. They also gave him the loyal army that proclaimed him Augustus at Paris in 360.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

set.detail:
Julian prepared a large invasion of Persia to avenge the defeats of Constantius' reign and establish his own glory. Leaving Antioch on 5 March 363, he sent an army of 30,000 under his relative Procopius and Sebastianus north to the Tigris to join the Armenian king Arsaces, while he himself led some 65,000 men down the Euphrates with a fleet of over 1,000 ships carrying supplies and siege equipment. Ammianus, who served in the campaign, describes the march past the tomb of Gordian III at Zaitha and the ruins of Dura, the capture of Anatha and of the fortresses of Pirisabora and Maiozamalcha, and the passage of the fleet through the canal of Trajan (Naarmalcha) to the Tigris.

In late May Julian defeated the Persian army before the walls of Ctesiphon, but the city was too strong to besiege and Shapur's main army was approaching. Julian ordered most of the fleet burned to avoid tying up 20,000 men to tow it upstream and turned inland, misled, Ammianus hints, by deserters, then found the country devastated by scorched-earth tactics. The army retreated north along the Tigris under constant harassment by cavalry and elephants. On 22 June it won a battle at Maranga, but on 26 June Julian was mortally wounded in a skirmish and died that night. Procopius' northern army never arrived.

Jovian, chosen emperor, led the army to Dura on the Tigris, where, short of food, he accepted a thirty-year peace ceding Nisibis, Singara and the five Transtigritane regions and abandoning Armenia. The campaign was the most ambitious Roman invasion of Persia since Severus and ended in the worst territorial loss in the east since Crassus. Ancient and modern critics blame Julian's overconfidence and decisions such as burning the fleet; others emphasise Persian strategy and the logistical difficulties.

scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

set.detail:
Procopius, a maternal relative of Julian born in Cilicia, had commanded the northern army in the Persian campaign of 363, and rumours spread that Julian had designated him as successor. Fearing Jovian and then Valentinian and Valens, he went into hiding. On 28 September 365, while Valens was in Bithynia on his way to Syria, Procopius persuaded two units passing through Constantinople, the Divitenses and the Tungricani Iuniores, to proclaim him emperor, appearing in a makeshift purple. He won over the capital by appealing to loyalty to the Constantinian dynasty, showing the troops the widow of Constantius II, Faustina, and her young daughter Constantia, and obtained 3,000 Gothic auxiliaries from Athanaric by claiming kinship with Constantine.

Valens, who had little support, considered abdicating, but was persuaded by his advisers to fight. Procopius' forces gained Thrace and Bithynia and besieged Nicaea and Chalcedon, but failed to win the Illyrian army. In spring 366 Valens, supported by veteran generals such as Arbitio, who persuaded Procopius' troops to desert, advanced through Phrygia. At Thyatira Procopius' general Gomoarius deserted, and at Nacolia Agilo did the same. Procopius fled, was betrayed by his own officers and executed on 27 May 366. His relative Marcellus briefly continued the revolt at Chalcedon before being captured and killed. Valens punished Procopius' supporters severely.

The revolt showed the continuing strength of loyalty to the Constantinian house and the fragility of the new Valentinianic dynasty. It also led to Valens' Gothic war of 367-369, waged against the Tervingi for having supported Procopius. Ammianus (book 26), Zosimus and Themistius' orations are the main sources.

scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

set.detail:
Valens waged war against the Tervingian Goths under Athanaric because they had sent troops to support Procopius, claiming the treaty of 332 bound them to the Constantinian family. In 367 Valens crossed the Danube on a bridge of boats near Transmarisca (Daphne) and ravaged Gothic territory, but the Goths withdrew into the mountains and avoided battle. In 368 the Danube floods prevented a crossing, and Valens wintered at Marcianopolis. In 369 he crossed near Noviodunum, advanced deep into Gothic territory, defeated the Greuthungi who came to Athanaric's aid, and drove Athanaric to sue for peace. The war also involved an economic blockade, cutting off trade with the Goths, which caused them hardship.

The peace was concluded in September 369 at a meeting on boats in the middle of the Danube, since Athanaric had sworn an oath never to set foot on Roman soil. The terms, praised by Themistius in his Oration 10, were less favourable to the Goths than those of 332: trade was restricted to two designated towns on the river, subsidies were apparently ended, and the Goths may no longer have been required to supply troops. Valens took the title Gothicus Maximus.

The war weakened the Tervingi and Athanaric's authority, contributing to internal divisions that included the persecution of Gothic Christians around 369-372 (the Passion of Saba the Goth describes it) and conflict between Athanaric and Fritigern. These divisions left the Tervingi vulnerable when the Huns attacked in the 370s, leading to the crossing of 376. Historians debate whether Valens' treaty of 369 was a diplomatic success or an unwise humiliation of an important client people.

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

set.detail:
Firmus was one of the sons of Nubel, a powerful Moorish chief in Mauretania Caesariensis who held a Roman command and was a Christian, possibly of Donatist sympathies. After Nubel's death around 370, a family conflict led Firmus to kill his half-brother Zammac, a friend of the corrupt comes Africae Romanus, whose oppression of the provinces Ammianus describes in detail. Fearing that Romanus' accusations would turn the emperor against him, Firmus revolted in 372, gaining the support of Moorish tribes and some Roman units, and was perhaps proclaimed emperor. His forces sacked Caesarea, the provincial capital, and attacked Icosium.

Valentinian sent his best general, the magister equitum Theodosius, father of the future emperor, who landed at Igilgili in 373 with a small army of Gallic veterans. Theodosius waged a difficult campaign in the mountains of Kabylia and the Atlas, negotiating with tribes and punishing defectors, including Roman soldiers, by mutilating them or burning them alive. Firmus' brothers were divided: Gildo sided with Rome, while Mascezel, Mazuca and others joined Firmus. After two years of war, the Isaflenses under King Igmazen, who had sheltered Firmus, agreed to hand him over; Firmus hanged himself in 375 to avoid capture, and his body was delivered to Theodosius on a camel.

The revolt revealed the tensions between Roman officials, local elites and Moorish chiefs in late Roman Africa. Theodosius' victory was followed by his own execution at Carthage in 376. Gildo became comes Africae and himself revolted in 397-398. Ammianus' account (29.5) is the main source; some historians (Frend) see links between Firmus and the Donatists, a view others reject.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Kotula, "Firmus, fils de Nubel", Eos 56 (1966)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

set.detail:
In 373 Valentinian ordered the building of a fort on Quadic territory north of the Danube. When the Quadic king Gabinius protested, the dux of Valeria, Marcellianus, invited him to a banquet and had him murdered. In 374 the outraged Quadi, joined by Sarmatians, crossed the Danube and devastated Pannonia and Valeria during the harvest. They nearly captured Constantia, the daughter of Constantius II and bride of Gratian, who was travelling to Gaul and was saved by the governor Messalla, who rushed her to Sirmium in a public carriage. The praetorian prefect Probus, at Sirmium, organised the defence of the city and cleaned out its ditches. The Sarmatians defeated and destroyed two legions, the Pannonica and the Moesiaca, while the young Theodosius, dux of Moesia Prima, defeated the Sarmatians in his sector.

In 375 Valentinian moved from Trier to Pannonia, crossed the Danube at Aquincum and ravaged Quadic territory, killing indiscriminately. In November the Quadi sent envoys to Brigetio to seek peace, claiming that the fort-building had provoked them and that the invaders were foreigners not under their control. Valentinian, enraged by their arguments, fell into a fit of fury and died of a stroke on 17 November 375.

The war illustrates Valentinian's aggressive frontier policy of building forts and bridgeheads across the rivers, which provoked conflicts with peoples beyond the frontier. It also shows the fragility of Roman control over the middle Danube on the eve of the Hunnic arrival. Ammianus (29.6 and 30.5-6) is the main source. The death of Valentinian left the west to the 16-year-old Gratian and the four-year-old Valentinian II.

scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

set.detail:
Pressed by the Huns, the Tervingi under Alavivus and Fritigern were admitted across the Danube in 376, while the Greuthungi of Alatheus and Saphrax crossed without permission. Exploitation by the Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus provoked a revolt; early in 377, after the attempt to murder the Gothic leaders at a banquet at Marcianople, Fritigern defeated Lupicinus nearby. Gothic soldiers in Roman service at Adrianople and miners from Thrace joined the rebels. In 377 Roman forces under Trajanus, Profuturus and Richomeres fought an indecisive battle at Ad Salices, and the Goths, reinforced by Huns and Alans, broke through the Haemus passes. Frigeridus and Sebastianus won smaller successes. On 9 August 378 Valens attacked the Gothic camp near Adrianople without waiting for Gratian and was killed with two-thirds of his army.

The Goths failed to take Adrianople and were repulsed from Constantinople, partly by Saracen cavalry; in the east the magister Julius massacred Gothic recruits and hostages. In 379 Gratian appointed Theodosius as Augustus for the east. Theodosius rebuilt the army, recruiting widely including Goths, and fought a war of attrition from Thessalonica; his general Modares, a Goth, won a victory in 379, but in 380 Theodosius was defeated in Macedonia, and Gratian's generals Bauto and Arbogast had to intervene. Gratian settled the Greuthungi in Pannonia in 380, and in January 381 Athanaric came to Constantinople and died there.

On 3 October 382 the magister Saturninus concluded a peace by which the Tervingi were settled in Thrace and northern Illyricum under their own leaders, providing troops when called upon. The war transformed Rome's relations with barbarians and is often seen as the beginning of the end for the western empire. Ammianus' book 31, Zosimus, Themistius and the church historians are the main sources.

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

set.detail:
In 383 the army in Britain proclaimed Magnus Maximus, who crossed to Gaul; Gratian's army deserted near Paris, and Gratian was killed at Lugdunum on 25 August 383. Maximus established his capital at Trier and controlled Britain, Gaul and Spain, while Valentinian II and his mother Justina ruled Italy, Africa and Illyricum from Milan. Theodosius, occupied in the east, recognised Maximus, and Ambrose conducted negotiations at Trier. Maximus presented himself as a champion of Nicene orthodoxy against the Homoian Justina and had the heretic Priscillian executed in 385.

In 387 Maximus invaded Italy, crossing the Alps behind envoys sent by Valentinian; Valentinian and Justina fled by sea from Aquileia to Thessalonica. Theodosius married Valentinian's sister Galla and prepared war. In the summer of 388 he advanced with an army that included Goths, Huns and Alans. Maximus' forces were defeated in two battles: at Siscia, where Theodosius' cavalry swam the Save and routed the enemy, and at Poetovio, where Maximus' brother Marcellinus was defeated. Theodosius pursued Maximus to Aquileia, where his soldiers handed him over; he was executed on 28 August 388. In Gaul, Arbogast killed Maximus' son Victor, and his general Andragathius drowned himself.

Theodosius restored Valentinian II in the west under the supervision of Arbogast and spent three years in Italy, visiting Rome in 389. Pacatus' panegyric of 389 celebrates the victory as the overthrow of a tyrant. The war showed the continued importance of the western armies' ability to choose emperors and the growing role of barbarian troops and generals, such as Arbogast, in imperial politics. Zosimus, Pacatus, Orosius, Sulpicius Severus and the church historians are the main sources.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court AD 364-425 (1975)
McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

set.detail:
After Maximus' defeat Theodosius left Valentinian II, then about seventeen, in the west under the Frankish magister militum Arbogast. Valentinian, residing at Vienne, resented Arbogast's control; when he handed Arbogast a letter of dismissal, the general tore it up, saying he had not received his command from the emperor. On 15 May 392 Valentinian was found hanged, whether by suicide or murder is disputed. Arbogast, unable as a barbarian to take the throne himself, proclaimed the rhetor and former official Flavius Eugenius emperor on 22 August 392. Eugenius, a Christian, sought recognition from Theodosius, who refused and in January 393 raised his younger son Honorius to Augustus.

In the west, Eugenius' regime allied with the pagan senatorial aristocracy, especially the praetorian prefect Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, who restored temples and festivals at Rome, and Ambrose left Milan to avoid contact with the usurper. In 394 Theodosius marched west with a large army including 20,000 Gothic federates under Gainas and Alaric, Huns, Alans and Iberians, with Stilicho and Timasius as generals. He crossed the Julian Alps unopposed and on 5-6 September 394 fought Eugenius and Arbogast at the river Frigidus. After heavy losses among the Goths on the first day, a fierce bora wind on the second day helped Theodosius' attack; Eugenius was captured and executed, Arbogast and Flavianus committed suicide.

Theodosius became sole ruler of the whole empire, but died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the east to Arcadius and the west to Honorius under Stilicho's guardianship. Christian writers presented the war as the final defeat of paganism, a view Alan Cameron has criticised as exaggerated. The heavy Gothic casualties contributed to the revolt of Alaric in 395.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans
Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
Croke, "Arbogast and the Death of Valentinian II", Historia 25 (1976)
